Just a bit of background on the report. On April 16th, 2025, the minimum energy regulations reverted to tier 1 of the National Building Code of Canada.
The province cited rising costs demand for affordable housing and alignment with energy standards in Alberta and Manitoba as key reasons for the change.
This change will result in step 1 of the low and low emissions community plan target to implement a step code for energy use no longer being met with in our small residential housing sector.

The report provides a detailed analysis on the implications and benefits associated with each energy tier as well as stakeholder preferences to regulate into tier 1 or tier 2 of the National Building Code and proposes two options for committees consideration.
To provide a bit of additional context on energy tiers, the purpose of energy tiers is to provide a clear pathway for improving energy efficiency of buildings over time.

By setting progressively higher building standards, the National Building Code aims to reduce environmental impact of buildings lower energy costs for occupants and contribute to a broader climate action goals.
Tier 2 represents a 10% energy performance improvement over tier 1 leading to utility savings improvements in home comfort and cleaner indoor air quality.
In terms of estimated cost of construction, tier 2 involves additional costs ranging from around 1100 to $3300 per home, but offers an estimated annual utility savings of $300.
In terms of greenhouse gas emissions, tier 2 aligns with the city's climate action goals resulting in significant greenhouse gas reductions.
Stakeholder engagement was undertaken to understand preferences for regulating to tier 1 or tier 2 with the full summary provided in the report.

Overall, feedback from stakeholders struck mixed opinions. Builders shared concerns about costs and their value for harmonized regulations across our province while environmental and housing organizations strongly supported at higher energy tiers for their long-term benefits.
Two options are being proposed for committee today. Option 1 is to maintain alignment with the low emissions community plan and regulate to tier 2.
This option involves regulating building energy standards, tier 2, which requires an amendment to the building by law.

The advantages of this option include alignment with our low emissions community plan targets, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, improved building quality, offers long-term cost reductions for residents and establish a Saskatoon as a leader in meeting environmental and climate change goals.
Key disadvantages include contributing to higher upfront costs and variability in the minimum energy requirements across our province.
Option 2 maintains alignment with the provincial regulations and regulates to tier 1.
This option contributes to low upfront costs and consistent regulation across the province.
It involves regulating building energy standards to tier 1 with builders having the option to voluntarily build to higher tiers.
The advantages of this option include the alignment across of regulations across our province and lower upfront costs compared to option 1.
The disadvantages include higher utility costs and may result in less efficient homes.
It would require other initiatives to be identified in order to meet the LAC plan targets.

This option outlines with our commitment to reduce greenhouse gases to net zero by 2050 and provides long-term benefits to homeowners and the environment.
